parts.latex:
Let $X$ be a uniform discrete random variable with possible values $X=1,2,3,\dots,n$.

Show that $\text{Var}(X)=\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}$.

You are given $1^2+2^2+3^2+\dots+n^2=\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$. [DO NOT PROVE THIS]

solutions.latex:
Each value has probability $P(X=x)=\dfrac1n$ for $x=1,2,\dots,n$.

Expected value, using $1+2+\dots+n=\dfrac n2(1+n)$:

$$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=1\times\dfrac1n+2\times\dfrac1n+\dots+n\times\dfrac1n\\&=\dfrac1n(1+2+\dots+n)\\&=\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac n2(1+n)\\&=\dfrac{1+n}{2}\end{aligned}$$

Using the given sum of squares:

$$\begin{aligned}E\left(X^2\right)&=\dfrac1n\left(1^2+2^2+\dots+n^2\right)\\&=\dfrac1n\cdot\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\\&=\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\text{Var}(X)=E\left(X^2\right)-\left(E(X)\right)^2$:

$$\begin{aligned}\text{Var}(X)&=\dfrac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}-\left(\dfrac{1+n}{2}\right)^2\\ &=\dfrac{(n+1)\left[2(2n+1)-3(1+n)\right]}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{(n+1)(n-1)}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{n^2-1}{12}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the $\text{Var}(X)$ formula and makes progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = \sin x$ at the origin?

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is the derivative at the origin.

$$y'=\cos x$$

When $x=0$, $y'=\cos 0=1$.

The tangent is

$$\begin{aligned} y-0 &= 1(x-0) \\ y &= x \end{aligned}$$

This is option D.

parts.latex: Given that $\log_a b = 3.75$ and $\log_a c = 0.25$. Find $\log_a (bc)^2$.

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws $\log_a x^2=2\log_a x$ and $\log_a(bc)=\log_a b+\log_a c$:

$$\begin{aligned} \log_a (bc)^2 &= 2\log_a(bc) \\ &= 2(\log_a b+\log_a c) \\ &= 2(3.75+0.25) \\ &= 8 \end{aligned}$$

This is option C.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\cos^2 3x$ with respect to $x$?

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $(\cos 3x)^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos^2 3x) &= 2\cos 3x\times(-3\sin 3x) \\ &= -6\sin 3x\cos 3x \end{aligned}$$

This is option A.

parts.latex:
The point $P(8, -3)$ lies on the graph of $y = f(x)$.

Find the coordinates of the image of $P$ if the function is transformed to

$$y = -2f(x+7) + 5.$$

solutions.latex:
Horizontal translation: $x+7$ shifts the graph left 7 units, so $x=8-7=1$.

Vertical dilation: multiply $y$ by $-2$, so $y=-3\times(-2)=6$.

Vertical translation: shift up 5 units, so $y=6+5=11$.

The image is $(1,11)$, which is option A.

parts.latex: Simplify $\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}-\dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{1-\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

This is option A.

parts.latex:
The third term of an arithmetic series is 32 and the sixth term is 17.

Find the sum of the first ten terms.

solutions.latex:
For an arithmetic series $T_n=a+(n-1)d$, so

$$\begin{aligned} a+2d &= 32 &&(1)\\ a+5d &= 17 &&(2) \end{aligned}$$

Subtracting, (1) $-$ (2): $-3d=15$, so $d=-5$ and $a=42$.

$$\begin{aligned} S_{10} &= \dfrac{10}{2}\left[2\times 42+9\times(-5)\right] \\ &= 195 \end{aligned}$$

This is option D.

4775.stem:
From the top of a tower, which is 60 metres high, Isaac throws a stone upward and allows it to fall under gravity.

The height of the stone is modelled by the equation, $h = 20t - 5t^2 + 60$, where $h$ is the height (in metres) of the stone above ground level and $t$ is the time in seconds since the stone was thrown.

figures.cap: blank grid of height h (metres) against time t (seconds) for drawing graphs
solution sketch: Stone parabola and Glider straight line drawn on the grid

parts.latex:
ON YOUR PAPER, NEATLY DRAW THE CURVE FOR THIS EQUATION AND LABEL IT “Stone”.

\exfigure{1316_q11_1}

At the same time as the stone is thrown, Jay releases a toy glider from the top of the tower.

The glider drifts down, losing height at a constant rate of 5 metres per second.

Draw the graph modelling the height of the glider on the grid on the previous page and determine the equation which describes the model. Label the graph Glider.
Determine the height of the glider when the stone reaches the ground.
can_use: Graphical solution of equations and inequalities

criteria: Correct parabolic graph for Stone, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric had one row of 1 mark though part is worth 2; made top-down with 2 marks.

solutions.latex:
The glider starts at the top of the tower, so the $h$-intercept is $c=60$.

It loses 5 m each second, so the gradient is

$$m=\dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}=-\dfrac{5}{1}=-5$$

The equation is

$$h=-5t+60$$
criteria: Correct straight-line graph for Glider, or correct equation

meta.format_note: The glider line is drawn on the graph in part (a)'s figure per source.

solutions.latex:
The stone reaches the ground when $t=6$.

$$\begin{aligned} h &= -5(6)+60 \\ &= 30 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

The glider is 30 metres high.

4777.stem: Differentiate the following with respect to $x$:

parts.latex: $\dfrac{\cos 3x}{x^2}$.
$\ln\sqrt{3-x}$.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=\cos 3x & v&=x^2\\ u'&=-3\sin 3x & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\cos 3x}{x^2}\right) &= \dfrac{-3x^2\sin 3x-2x\cos 3x}{(x^2)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x(-3x\sin 3x-2\cos 3x)}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{-3x\sin 3x-2\cos 3x}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using log laws to simplify first:

$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= \ln\sqrt{3-x} \\ &= \ln (3-x)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(3-x) \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{-1}{3-x} \\ &= \dfrac{-1}{2(3-x)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses log laws, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int (3x-4)^8\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the reverse chain rule for a linear function of $x$ (divide by the power and the coefficient of $x$):

$$\begin{aligned} \int (3x-4)^8\,dx &= \dfrac{(3x-4)^9}{9\times 3}+C \\ &= \dfrac{(3x-4)^9}{27}+C \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source rubric had two rows of 1 mark (noting guidelines allocate 2) though paper prints 1 mark; reduced to the single paper mark.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{4\sin\left(\frac{5x}{3}\right)}{7}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
The integral of $\sin kx$ is $-\dfrac{1}{k}\cos kx$, so adjust for the coefficient $\dfrac{5}{3}$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{4\sin\left(\frac{5x}{3}\right)}{7}\,dx &= \dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{3}{5}\int\dfrac{5}{3}\sin\left(\dfrac{5x}{3}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{12}{35}\left(-\cos\dfrac{5x}{3}\right)+C \\ &= -\dfrac{12}{35}\cos\left(\dfrac{5x}{3}\right)+C \end{aligned}$$

4780.stem:
A block of land is in the shape of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ shown below. The diagonal $AC$ has been drawn.

The following measurements have been taken:

$AD = 75$ m, $BC = 90$ m.

$D$ is 135 m due south of $B$.

$\angle CAD = 53^\circ$ and $\angle ACD = 32^\circ$.

\exfigure{1316_q15_1}

figures.cap: quadrilateral ABCD with diagonal AC, BD vertical north-south of 135 m

parts.latex: Find the length of $CD$. (Answer correct to the nearest metre.)

Find the size of $\angle CBD$ and hence give the bearing of $C$ from $B$.

(Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.)

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle ACD$, using the sine rule:

$$\dfrac{CD}{\sin 53^\circ}=\dfrac{75}{\sin 32^\circ}$$

$$\begin{aligned} CD &= \dfrac{75\sin 53^\circ}{\sin 32^\circ} \\ &= 113.03167727\ldots \\ &\approx 113 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the sine rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle BCD$, using the cosine rule with $CD\approx 113$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle CBD &= \dfrac{90^2+135^2-113^2}{2\times 90\times 135} \\ &= \dfrac{13556}{24300} \\ &= 0.55786008\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \angle CBD &= \cos^{-1}(0.55786008) \\ &= 56.092\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 56^\circ \end{aligned}$$

$D$ is due south of $B$, so the bearing of $C$ from $B$ is

$$180^\circ-56^\circ=124^\circ$$
criteria: Correct use of the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric (2 + 1 + 1 marks, noting guidelines allocate 2 in total, paper prints 3) rewritten top-down out of 3, the paper's mark. Original 13556/24300 simplification kept; $90^2+135^2-113^2=13556$ checked.

BD drawn as a fine aux dashed N-S line with a gap for '135 m', continuing up to a filled -latex north arrow (crop's open chevron replaced, rule 4). Angle arcs at A (53°) and C (32°) are true arcs centred on the vertices, ending on both arms. Positions match the crop's layout (rule 1). Lines 0.6pt.

parts.latex:
Ten kilograms of salt is placed into a swimming pool and begins to dissolve.

After $t$ hours the amount, $S$ kg, of undissolved salt is given by: $S = 10e^{-kt}$.

Calculate the value of $k$ to 3 significant figures, given that $S = 4.7$ when $t = 4$.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $S=4.7$ and $t=4$ into $S=10e^{-kt}$:

$$4.7=10e^{-4k}$$

$$\dfrac{4.7}{10}=e^{-4k}$$

Taking natural logs:

$$\begin{aligned} -4k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{4.7}{10}\right) \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{4.7}{10}\right)}{-4} \\ &= 0.1887556461\ldots \\ &\approx 0.189 \end{aligned}$$

4782.stem:
Lachlan works in a Moolworths store and he is making a stack of oranges against a sloping display panel.

The oranges are stacked in layers, as shown, where each layer contains one orange less than the layer below it.

\exfigure{1316_q17_1}

When he has finished, there are five oranges in the top layer, six in the next and so on.

There are $n$ layers altogether.

figures.cap: stack of oranges in layers, top layer to nth layer

parts.latex: Show there are $\dfrac{1}{2}n(n+9)$ oranges in the stack.
If Lachlan has 300 oranges to create his display, how many full rows can he create, if the top row still contains five oranges?

solutions.latex:
The numbers of oranges form an arithmetic series $5+6+7+\cdots+(n+4)$, with first term $a=5$, common difference $d=1$ and last term $l=n+4$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$:

$$\begin{aligned} S_n &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left[5+(n+4)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{n}{2}(n+9) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}n(n+9) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Establishes the series and uses the correct formula, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Set the sum equal to 300:

$$\begin{aligned} 300 &= \dfrac{1}{2}n(n+9) \\ 600 &= n^2+9n \\ 0 &= n^2+9n-600 \end{aligned}$$

Using the quadratic formula:

$$n=\dfrac{-9\pm\sqrt{81-4\times 1\times(-600)}}{2}$$

So $n\approx 20.4$ or $n\approx -29.4$. Since $n>0$ and must be a whole number of rows, take $n=20.4$ and round down.

$$\therefore\ \text{Lachlan can make 20 complete rows.}$$
criteria: Sets up the correct quadratic equation, or equivalent merit

1316_q17_1.notes: Stack of oranges: 5/6/7 circles in offset rows, two groups of 3 for the nth layer, fine dashed double-headed vertical arrows and horizontal arrows with '?' labels, all filled latex heads (rule 4). Original-cover score 0.84 is just under target only because the scan strokes are heavier than 0.6pt and the text shifts a little.

parts.latex: Solve $2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) = 1$ for the domain $[-\pi, \pi]$.

solutions.latex:
Rearrange first:

$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= 1 \\ \sin^2\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right) &= \pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned}$$

For $-\pi\le x\le\pi$, we need $-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\le\dfrac{x}{3}\le\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

The only solutions in this interval are $\dfrac{x}{3}=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

The other solutions, $\pm\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$, lie outside it (giving $x=\pm\dfrac{9\pi}{4}$, outside the domain).

$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\text{ or } x=-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$$
criteria: Rearranges the equation and finds $\dfrac{x}{3}$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: By first differentiating $\ln(\cos x)$, find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \tan x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating using the chain rule:

$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln(\cos x)=\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}=-\tan x$$

So $\tan x$ has antiderivative $-\ln(\cos x)$.

$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\tan x\,dx &= -\left[\ln\cos x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &= -\left[\ln\dfrac{1}{2}-\ln 1\right] \\ &= -\ln\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \ln 2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x+5}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2-6x+5)=2x-6=2(x-3)$, the numerator is half the derivative of the denominator.

Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln f(x)+C$:

$$\begin{aligned} \int\dfrac{x-3}{x^2-6x+5}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{2(x-3)}{x^2-6x+5}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|x^2-6x+5\right|+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates the denominator and recognises $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln f(x)$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote $\ln(x^2-6x+5)$ without absolute value; added modulus signs since $x^2-6x+5$ can be negative (formatting-level correction, same method).

parts.latex:
By using the Trapezoidal rule with 4 sub intervals, estimate the integral

$$\int_0^{\frac{1}{2}} \sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx.$$

solutions.latex: \extable{Ts7100_1}

meta.format_note: Table content is in the table Ts7100_1; values not visible here, not checked.

solutions.latex:
Here $a=0$, $b=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and there are 4 sub-intervals, so the strip width is
$$h=\dfrac{b-a}{n}=\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}-0}{4}=0.125$$
Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{1}{2}}\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(a)+f(b)+2\big(f(x_1)+f(x_2)+f(x_3)\big)\right]$$
Substituting the table values:
$$\begin{aligned} &\approx\dfrac{0.125}{2}\left[(1+0.866)+2(0.992+0.968+0.927)\right] \\ &\approx 0.4775 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the trapezoidal rule and substitutes appropriate values, or equivalent merit

4787.stem:
Two websites give reviews of books.

Both sites give each book a rating out of a possible 100.

A statistician analysed the ratings awarded by the two sites to 100 books and obtained the statistical results below.

\extable{1316_q22_t1}

parts.latex:
The book “Moonlighting” got a rating of 78 on Bookophile and a rating of 84 on Great Reads.

Convert both these ratings to $z$-scores and determine which website rated the book higher in comparison to other books on the site.
What percentage of books would have a rating between 60 and 84 on the Bookophile website?

solutions.latex:
Using the $z$-score formula $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} z_B&=\dfrac{78-60}{12}=\dfrac{18}{12}=1.5 \\ z_G&=\dfrac{84-76}{8}=\dfrac{8}{8}=1 \end{aligned}$$
Since $1.5>1$, the rating on Bookophile is higher in comparison to other books on the site.
criteria: At least one $z$-score correct and correct conclusion, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
On Bookophile the $z$-scores are:
$$\begin{aligned} x=60:\ z&=\dfrac{60-60}{12}=0 \\ x=84:\ z&=\dfrac{84-60}{12}=2 \end{aligned}$$
Approximately $95\%$ of scores have $z$-scores between $-2$ and $2$, so by symmetry $47.5\%$ lie between $z=0$ and $z=2$.
$$\therefore\ 47.5\%\text{ of books}$$
criteria: Uses one correct and relevant percentage, or equivalent merit

4788.stem:
Consider the probability density function for a random variable $X$ given by:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{k}{\sqrt{9+3x}} & 0 \le x \le 9 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$ and hence write the equation of the Cumulative Density Function.
Find the median value of $X$.

solutions.latex:
For a probability density function the total area is 1:
$$\displaystyle\int_0^9\dfrac{k}{\sqrt{9+3x}}\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[\dfrac{(9+3x)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{3\times\frac{1}{2}}\right]_0^9&=1 \\ \dfrac{2k}{3}\left[(9+27)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9^{\frac{1}{2}}\right]&=1 \\ \dfrac{2k}{3}\left[6-3\right]&=1 \\ 2k&=1 \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_0^x(9+3t)^{-\frac{1}{2}}dt \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{(9+3t)^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}\times 3}\right]_0^x \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}(9+3x)^{\frac{1}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{3}(9)^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3x}-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{2},\qquad F(x)=\dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3x}-1\ \text{ for } 0\le x\le 9$$
criteria: Correct value of $k$, or equivalent merit
Sets the integral equal to 1 and integrates, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The median $m$ satisfies $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9+3m}-1&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \sqrt{9+3m}&=\dfrac{9}{2} \\ 9+3m&=\dfrac{81}{4} \\ 3m&=\dfrac{45}{4} \\ m&=\dfrac{15}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{median}=\dfrac{15}{4}$$
criteria: Realises the median is found by setting $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, or equivalent merit

4789.stem:
A sector of a circle, centre $O$, is shown below.

The points $A$ and $B$ lie on the circle, such that the length of the chord $AB$ is 104 metres, and the length of the arc $AB$ is 126 metres.

The radius is $r$ metres and the angle subtended at the centre by the arc is $2\alpha$ radians.

\exfigure{1316_q24_1}

figures.cap: sector with chord AB 104 m, arc AB 126 m, angle 2alpha at O
solution sketch: right-angled triangle with 52 and angle alpha, hypotenuse r

parts.latex: Show that $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{52\alpha}{63}$.

If $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, find the exact radius of the circle.

Express your answer with a rational denominator.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1316_q24_s1}

The perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$ bisects the chord and the angle $2\alpha$. In the right-angled triangle, half the chord is $52$, so
$$\sin\alpha=\dfrac{52}{r}\quad\text{so}\quad r=\dfrac{52}{\sin\alpha}\qquad(1)$$
Arc length $l=r\theta$ with $\theta=2\alpha$:
$$126=2\alpha r\quad\text{so}\quad r=\dfrac{63}{\alpha}\qquad(2)$$
Equating (1) and (2):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{63}{\alpha}&=\dfrac{52}{\sin\alpha} \\ 63\sin\alpha&=52\alpha \\ \sin\alpha&=\dfrac{52\alpha}{63} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up two equations for $r$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using $r=\dfrac{52}{\sin\alpha}$ with $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned} r&=\dfrac{52}{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}} \\ &=52\div\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=52\times\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{104}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=\dfrac{104\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ r=\dfrac{104\sqrt{3}}{3}\text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds $r$ correctly using either equation for $r$, or equivalent merit

1316_q24_1.notes: Sector OAB: true circular arc centred at O through A and B, chord AB, equal-length tick marks on OA and OB, a 2α angle arc at O, and labels 126 m, 104 m, r. α is in maths italic (rule 19); the crop's α is upright. Score just under 0.85 is due to the scan's heavier strokes.

1316_q24_s1.notes: Solution right triangle: top side 52, hypotenuse r, angle α at the bottom-right vertex. The α arc is a true arc centred on that vertex, running from the hypotenuse to the vertical side. Lines are 0.6pt where the scan's are heavy (rule 3), and that is what drops the original-cover score. α is in maths italic (rule 19).

parts.latex: Show with calculations why this geometric series has a limiting sum.
Find the exact value of the limiting sum with a rational denominator.

solutions.latex:
A geometric series has a limiting sum when $|r|<1$, where $r=\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$.
$$r=\dfrac{\sqrt{7}-2}{1}=\sqrt{7}-2\approx 0.6$$
Since $|r|<1$, the series has a limiting sum.

With $a=1$ and $r=\sqrt{7}-2$, the limiting sum formula is $S=\dfrac{a}{1-r}$.
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{1}{1-(\sqrt{7}-2)} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{3-\sqrt{7}}\times\dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{3+\sqrt{7}} \\ &=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{9-7} \\ &=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{7}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct formula and substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Calculate Pearson’s correlation coefficient for the data, correct to two decimal places.

parts.latex: Describe the direction and strength of the relationship between the IQ scores and the test marks.

parts.latex:
The equation of the least-squares regression line is:

$$M = 0.615I + b$$

where $M$ is the test mark, $I$ is the IQ score and $b$ is the intercept on the $M$-axis.

Find the value of $b$ and use the least-squares regression line to predict the test mark of a student who recorded an IQ of 114. (Answer as a whole number.)
parts.note: Least-squares regression is not in 2024 Advanced; it is Mathematics Standard content.

solutions.latex:
Using a calculator:
$$r=0.98207928\ldots\approx 0.98\ \text{(to 2 decimal places)}$$
Since $r$ is positive and close to 1, there is a strong positive correlation between IQ scores and test marks.

The least-squares line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$. From the calculator, $\bar{I}=99.2$ and $\bar{M}=83.2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 83.2&=0.615(99.2)+b \\ 83.2&=61.008+b \\ b&=22.192 \end{aligned}$$
The line is $M=0.615I+22.192$.

For $I=114$:
$$\begin{aligned} M&=0.615(114)+22.192 \\ &=70.11+22.192 \\ &=92.302 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the estimated test mark is } 92$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $b$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Reading the value directly from the regression line on the calculator gives $b=22.176$.
meta.format_note: Source labelled the means $\bar{x}$, $\bar{y}$; written here as $\bar{I}$, $\bar{M}$ to match the question's variables.

parts.latex: Based on your answers to (a) and (b), determine which option would cost Jamie-Lee less each year in payments.
parts.note: Comparison built on the interest-factor table answers from (a) and (b); table look-ups are Standard content.

parts.latex: Outline one other factor she should consider when comparing these options.
parts.note: Qualitative comparison of the table-based annuity/loan options; part of removed interest-factor table question.

solutions.latex:
From the table, for $3\%$ and $15$ years the interest factor is $18.5989$.

The yearly investment $A$ satisfies $18.5989A=250\,000$:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=250\,000\div 18.5989 \\ &=13\,441.655\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{yearly investment}=\$13\,441.66$$

The monthly rate is $3\%\div 12=0.25\%$ and the period is $15\times 12=180$ months, so the table interest factor is $144.8055$.

If $R$ is the monthly repayment, $250\,000=144.8055R$.
$$\begin{aligned} R&=250\,000\div 144.8055 \\ &=\$1726.45 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{monthly repayment}=\$1726.45$$
criteria: Correct interest factor, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Loan payments per year:
$$\begin{aligned} 1726.45\times 12&=\$20\,717.45 \end{aligned}$$
This is more than the yearly investment of $\$13\,441.66$.

Therefore she would pay less each year with the investment option.

Other factors that need to be considered include:

The price of the property could increase significantly over 15 years.

Rent would be saved by buying a property now through a loan.

Inflation could change the relative value of $\$250\,000$ over 15 years.

4793.stem:
Two curves $y = 2e^{-x}$ and $y = e^x - 1$ intersect at a point $P$.

\exfigure{1316_q28_1}

figures.cap: curves y=2e^-x and y=e^x-1 meeting at P
solution sketch: graph of the two curves with the region bounded with y-axis shaded

parts.latex: Show, algebraically, that the coordinates of $P$ are $(\ln 2, 1)$.
Find the area bounded by the two curves and the $y$-axis.

solutions.latex:
At an intersection the $y$-values are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{-x}&=e^x-1 \\ \dfrac{2}{e^x}&=e^x-1 \\ 2&=e^{2x}-e^x \\ e^{2x}-e^x-2&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $m=e^x$:
$$\begin{aligned} m^2-m-2&=0 \\ (m-2)(m+1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $e^x=2$ or $e^x=-1$. Since $e^x>0$, $e^x\neq -1$, so $x=\ln 2$.

When $x=\ln 2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=2e^{-\ln 2} \\ &=2\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P=(\ln 2,\,1)$$
criteria: Reaches the quadratic equation to solve, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1316_q28_s1}

The area is the area under $y=2e^{-x}$ minus the area under $y=e^x-1$, from $x=0$ to $x=\ln 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\displaystyle\int_0^{\ln 2}2e^{-x}\,dx-\int_0^{\ln 2}(e^x-1)\,dx \\ &=\Big[-2e^{-x}\Big]_0^{\ln 2}-\Big[e^x-x\Big]_0^{\ln 2} \\ &=(-2e^{-\ln 2}+2)-\big[(e^{\ln 2}-\ln 2)-(e^0-0)\big] \\ &=(-1+2)-(2-\ln 2-1) \\ &=1-(1-\ln 2) \\ &=\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=\ln 2\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Finds the area under the curves, or draws an appropriate diagram to solve, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: triangular pdf graph, peak 0.5 at x=2, zero at x=4

solutions.latex:
The area under the triangle is
$$A=\dfrac{1}{2}bh=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 0.5=1\text{ unit}^2$$
So $\displaystyle\int_0^4 f(x)\,dx=1$, and $f(x)=0$ outside $(0,4)$, so $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1$. Also $f(x)\ge 0$, so it could be a probability density function.

For $0\le x<2$: the gradient is $m=\dfrac{0.5}{2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and the $y$-intercept is $0$, so $y=\dfrac{x}{4}$.

For $2\le x\le 4$: the gradient is $m=\dfrac{-0.5}{2}=-\dfrac{1}{4}$, and $y=0$ when $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-0&=-\dfrac{1}{4}(x-4) \\ y&=1-\dfrac{x}{4} \end{aligned}$$
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x}{4} & 0\le x<2\\[6pt] 1-\dfrac{x}{4} & 2\le x\le 4\\[6pt] 0 & \text{for all other values of } x\end{cases}$$
criteria: Finds the two equations, or equivalent merit

4795.stem: A particle is moving so that its velocity in m/s is given by $v = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.latex: Find the displacement equation $x$ in terms of $t$ for this particle.
Find the exact distance travelled in the first 4 seconds.
Find the exact acceleration of the particle at $t = 4$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$x=\displaystyle\int\left(1-2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right)dt=t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=0-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin 0+C \\ C&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$$
criteria: Correct integral to find $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-2\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}&=0 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi t}{3}&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{\pi t}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3},\dfrac{7\pi}{3} \\ t&=1,5,7 \end{aligned}$$
In the first 4 seconds the direction changes only at $t=1$, so find the distance for $0\le t\le 1$ and $1\le t\le 4$ separately.
$$\begin{aligned} d&=\left|\displaystyle\int_0^1 v\,dt\right|+\left|\displaystyle\int_1^4 v\,dt\right| \\ &=\left|\left[t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right]_0^1\right|+\left|\left[t-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}\right]_1^4\right| \\ &=\left|1-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right|+\left|\left(4+\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\left(1-\dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &=\left|1-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right|+\left|3+\dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right| \\ &=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi}-1+3+\dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\ &=2+\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\left(2+\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right)\text{ m}$$
criteria: Allows for the change of direction and sets up the appropriate sum of integrals, or equivalent merit
Finds the endpoints of motion, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:
$$a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{3}$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \\ &=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,\pi}{3}\text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Differentiates to find the acceleration, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: cone with slant height 13 cm, height h, radius r

solutions.latex:
In the cone, Pythagoras' theorem gives $r^2+h^2=169$, so $r^2=169-h^2$.

Substituting into $V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi(169-h^2)h \\ &=\dfrac{169\pi h}{3}-\dfrac{\pi h^3}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $V'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} V'&=\dfrac{169\pi}{3}-\pi h^2=0 \\ h^2&=\dfrac{169}{3} \\ h&=\dfrac{13}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{13\sqrt{3}}{3}\approx 7.5 \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature with the second derivative:
$$V''=-2\pi h<0\ \text{ when } h=\dfrac{13\sqrt{3}}{3}$$
so it is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ h=\dfrac{13\sqrt{3}}{3}\text{ cm}$$
criteria: Finds the first derivative and the stationary point, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $r$ into the volume formula, or equivalent merit
Finds an equation for $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Write down the domain
Find the horizontal and vertical asymptotes

solutions.latex:
The denominator must not be zero: $x^2-4\neq 0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{domain: all real } x,\ x\neq\pm 2$$

Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero: $x=\pm 2$.

For the horizontal asymptote:
$$\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\dfrac{8}{x^2-4}=0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{vertical asymptotes } x=\pm 2,\ \text{horizontal asymptote } y=0$$
criteria: Correct vertical or horizontal asymptotes (either), or equivalent merit

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn sketch of f(x)=2x^3-x^4 on [-2,2] with key points

parts.latex:
Consider the function $f(x) = 2x^3 - x^4$

Sketch the function for the domain $[-2,2]$, showing all key features including finding any stationary points, determining the nature and or any inflexions.

Space to draw the graph is provided on the next page.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur when $f'(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x)&=6x^2-4x^3 \\ &=2x^2(3-2x)=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$. Then $f(0)=0$ and $f\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)=\dfrac{27}{16}$.

The stationary points are $(0,0)$ and $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$.

Nature, from the sign of $f'(x)$:

\extable{Ts7127_1}

So $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion and $\left(\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{27}{16}\right)$ is a maximum turning point.

For other inflexions, $f''(x)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} f''(x)&=12x-12x^2 \\ &=12x(1-x)=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=0$ or $x=1$.

\extable{Ts7127_2}

The concavity changes at $x=1$ and $f(1)=1$, so $(1,1)$ is a point of inflexion. $(0,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion, as found above.

\exfigure{1316_q33_s1}

parts.latex: Simplify: $\dfrac{x^2+x-30}{x^2-19x-150}$

solutions.latex:
Factorise the numerator and the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2+x-30 &= (x+6)(x-5) \\ x^2-19x-150 &= (x+6)(x-25) \end{aligned}$$
Cancel the common factor $x+6$.
$$\dfrac{(x+6)(x-5)}{(x+6)(x-25)}=\dfrac{x-5}{x-25}$$
This matches option D.

meta.format_note: Source's denominator factorisation (x+6)(x-25) was stated without working; expanded briefly. Check: (x+6)(x-25)=x^2-19x-150.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\log_e(x^2+2)$

solutions.latex:
Using the chain rule on $y=\ln(x^2+2)$, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\ln u=\dfrac{u'}{u}$ with $u=x^2+2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{1}{x^2+2}\times 2x \\ &= \dfrac{2x}{x^2+2} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: The random variable $X$ is distributed normally with $\mu=12$ and $\sigma=2$, and the random variable $Z$, has a standard normal distribution. Which of the following is true?

solutions.latex:
Standardise using $Z=\dfrac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$.
$$\begin{aligned} Z &= \dfrac{9-12}{2} \\ &= -\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
So $P(X<9)=P(Z<-1.5)$.

By symmetry of the standard normal distribution, $P(Z<-1.5)=P(Z>1.5)$.

This matches option A.

parts.latex: The inequality which defines the domain of the function $f(x)=\dfrac{-4}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}$ is:

solutions.latex:
The square root needs $9-x^2>0$, and it is in the denominator so it cannot be zero.
$$\begin{aligned} 9-x^2 &> 0 \\ (3-x)(3+x) &> 0 \end{aligned}$$
The parabola $9-x^2$ is positive between its roots.
$$-3<x<3$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: The mass $Q$, in grams, of a certain radioactive isotope is given by $Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$, where $Q_0$ and $k$ are positive constants. If the mass of the isotope halves every 20 years, approximately how many years would it take for this isotope to decay 85% of its initial mass?

solutions.latex:
Halving every 20 years gives $Q=\dfrac{Q_0}{2}$ when $t=20$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{Q_0}{2} &= Q_0e^{-20k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= e^{-20k} \\ \ln\dfrac{1}{2} &= -20k \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{20}\ln\dfrac{1}{2}\approx 0.035 \end{aligned}$$
Decaying $85\%$ leaves $15\%$ of the mass.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.15Q_0 &= Q_0e^{-kt} \\ \ln 0.15 &= -kt \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 0.15}{-0.035}\approx 54.74 \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

Use conditional probability: given the student likes volleyball, find the probability they are a junior.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{junior}\mid\text{likes volleyball}) &= \dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)} \\ &= \dfrac{310}{605} \\ &= \dfrac{62}{121} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex:
The graph below shows the functions $f(x)=-3$ and $g(x)=x^2(x-2)$. The curves intersect at the point $(-1,-3)$. What is the area of the shaded region?

\exfigure{1317_q7_1}

solutions.latex:
Expand $g(x)=x^2(x-2)=x^3-2x^2$.

The shaded region lies between $g(x)$ and $f(x)=-3$ from the intersection at $x=-1$ to $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \left|\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}\left(x^3-2x^2+3\right)dx\right| \\ &= \left|\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-\dfrac{2}{3}x^3+3x\right]_{-1}^{0}\right| \\ &= \left|0-\left(\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{2}{3}-3\right)\right| \\ &= \left|0-\left(-\dfrac{25}{12}\right)\right| \\ &= \dfrac{25}{12} \text{ square units} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

solutions.latex:
Four sub-intervals on $0\le x\le 20$ give $h=\dfrac{20-0}{4}=5$, so the $x$ values are $0,5,10,15,20$.

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{h}{2}\left[f(0)+2f(5)+2f(10)+2f(15)+f(20)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{5}{2}\left[2+2\times 4.5+2\times 5.1+2\times 3.6+0\right] \\ &= \dfrac{5}{2}\times 28.4 \\ &= 71 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: The velocity of a particle is given by $v(t)=-9\cos 3t$ for $0\le t\le 2\pi$, where $v$ is measured in metres per second and time is measured in seconds. After $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ seconds, the particle has a displacement of $5$ metres. What is the equation of the displacement of the particle?

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} x(t) &= \displaystyle\int -9\cos 3t\,dt \\ &= -\dfrac{9\sin 3t}{3}+c \\ &= -3\sin 3t+c \end{aligned}$$
Use $x=5$ when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 5 &= -3\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{6}+c \\ &= -3\times 1+c \\ c &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
So $x(t)=-3\sin 3t+8$, which is option C.

options.latex: The function is not continuous at $x=0$.

parts.latex: Which of the following statements is true for the function $f(x)=e^{\frac{2}{x}}-1$?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$f'(x)=-\dfrac{2}{x^2}e^{\frac{2}{x}}$$
A: $f'(1)=-2e^2$ exists, so $f$ is differentiable at $x=1$. A is false.

B: $f(0)$ is undefined because of $e^{\frac{2}{0}}$, so $f$ is not continuous at $x=0$. B is true.

C: $f'(x)=0$ has no solution, so there is no stationary point. C is false.

D: as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$, $f(x)\to 0$, so the horizontal asymptote is $y=0$, not $y=-1$. D is false.

Hence the answer is option B.

parts.latex: Find the value of $p$ and $q$ such that $(1-\sqrt{3})^2=2p-\sqrt{3q}$

solutions.latex:
Expand the left-hand side.
$$\begin{aligned} (1-\sqrt{3})^2 &= (1-\sqrt{3})(1-\sqrt{3}) \\ &= 1-2\sqrt{3}+3 \\ &= 4-2\sqrt{3} \\ &= 2(2)-\sqrt{3\times 4} \end{aligned}$$
Comparing with $2p-\sqrt{3q}$:
$$\therefore\ p=2,\ q=4$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $|3x+4|=5$.

solutions.latex:
Split into the two cases.
$$3x+4=5 \quad\text{or}\quad 3x+4=-5$$
$$3x=1 \quad\text{or}\quad 3x=-9$$
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ or } x=-3$$

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{5x^2-3x}{x^3}\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Divide each term by $x^3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int\dfrac{5x^2-3x}{x^3}\,dx &= \int\left(\dfrac{5}{x}-3x^{-2}\right)dx \\ &= 5\ln|x|-\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}+C \\ &= 5\ln|x|+\dfrac{3}{x}+C \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer (mark still awarded if no absolute value signs)
One term correct, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\cos 2x}{e^x}\right)$ in simplest form.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\cos 2x & v&=e^x \\ u'&=-2\sin 2x & v'&=e^x \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{\cos 2x}{e^x}\right) &= \dfrac{e^x(-2\sin 2x)-\cos 2x\,(e^x)}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{e^x(-2\sin 2x-\cos 2x)}{(e^x)^2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{e^x}\left(-2\sin 2x-\cos 2x\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric rewritten top-down; the 1-mark row combines the source's quotient rule mark.

parts.latex: Solve for $x$: $\log_3(2x+1)+\log_3 x=1$

solutions.latex:
Combine the logarithms using $\log_a m+\log_a n=\log_a(mn)$. The logarithms need $2x+1>0$ and $x>0$, so $x>0$.
$$\log_3\big(x(2x+1)\big)=1$$
Convert to index form.
$$\begin{aligned} x(2x+1) &= 3^1 \\ 2x^2+x-3 &= 0 \\ 2x^2-2x+3x-3 &= 0 \\ 2x(x-1)+3(x-1) &= 0 \\ (2x+3)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=1$ or $x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Since $x>0$, $x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x=1$$
criteria: Progress towards a solution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\sqrt{3}\sin\theta+\cos\theta=0$ where $0\le\theta\le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Rearranging, $\sqrt3\sin\theta=-\cos\theta$.

Dividing by $\cos\theta$ (note $\cos\theta\ne 0$, since otherwise $\sin\theta=0$ as well):
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \\ \tan\theta&=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3} \end{aligned}$$
The tangent is negative in the second and fourth quadrants, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$$\therefore\ \theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
criteria: Makes progress towards a solution, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added short note on why cos θ is nonzero and quadrant reasoning; degrees form dropped in favour of radians (same values: 150°, 330°).

parts.latex: If the median of the distribution is $4$, write down the minimum possible value of $k$.
If the mean of the distribution is $3$, find the value of $k$.

solutions.latex:
Writing the data in order from the largest value, the sample has $k+16$ values.

$$5,5,5,5,4,4,4,4,\underline{4},3,3,3,3,3,3,3,2,\dots$$
There are 8 numbers on each side of the median (the underlined $4$).

$$\therefore\ k=1$$

meta.format_note: Source says 'circled 4'; shown as underlined. Source working is brief; kept as is. Minimum k = 1 as given.

solutions.latex:
The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{mean}&=\dfrac{2k+3\times 7+4\times 5+5\times 4}{k+16} \\ 3&=\dfrac{2k+61}{k+16} \\ 3k+48&=2k+61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=13$$

4816.stem: A curve $C$ has the equation $y=f(x)$ where $x\neq 0$. The point $P(1,3)$ lies on the curve.

parts.latex: Find $f(x)$, given $f'(x)=7-\dfrac{3}{x^2}+4x$

Find the equation of the normal to curve $C$, at the point $P$.

Express your answer in general form.

solutions.latex:
Integrating $f'(x)=7-3x^{-2}+4x$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(x)&=\int\left(7-3x^{-2}+4x\right)dx \\ &=7x-\dfrac{3x^{-1}}{-1}+\dfrac{4x^2}{2}+c \\ &=2x^2+7x+\dfrac3x+c \end{aligned}$$
Since $P(1,3)$ lies on the curve:
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=2+7+3+c \\ c&=-9 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ f(x)=2x^2+7x+\dfrac3x-9$$

meta.marker_note: Allow carry-on error for the final mark.

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent at $P$ is $f'(1)$:
$$m_T=7-3+4=8$$
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so $m_N=-\dfrac18$.

Equation of the normal:
$$\begin{aligned} y-3&=-\dfrac18(x-1) \\ 8y-24&=-x+1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x+8y-25=0$$
criteria: Finds the gradient of the normal, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Standardise using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\ge 18)&=P\left(Z\ge\dfrac{18-5}{10}\right) \\ &=P(Z\ge 1.3) \\ &=1-P(Z<1.3) \\ &=1-0.9032 \\ &=0.0968 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X\ge 18)=0.0968=\dfrac{121}{1250}$$

figures.cap: graph of velocity v = -sin(pi t/4) for 0 <= t <= 8

parts.latex: Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first $6$ seconds.
At what time does the particle reach its maximum displacement? Justify your answer.

solutions.latex:
From the graph, $v\le 0$ for $0\le t\le 4$ and $v\ge 0$ for $4\le t\le 8$, and the graph is symmetric about $t=4$. The distance in the first 4 seconds equals the distance in the last 4, so the first 6 seconds cover $1.5$ times the first 4 seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=\left|\int_0^4\left(-\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right)dt\right|\times 1.5 \\ &=\left|\left[\dfrac{4}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{4}\right]_0^4\right|\times 1.5 \\ &=\left|\dfrac4\pi\cos\pi-\dfrac4\pi\cos 0\right|\times 1.5 \\ &=\left|-\dfrac8\pi\right|\times 1.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\dfrac{12}{\pi}\text{ m}$$

meta.format_note: Added a short explanation of the symmetry factor 1.5; mathematics unchanged.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is position relative to the origin.

Integrating the velocity gives $x=\dfrac{4}{\pi}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right)+c$.

Maximum displacement occurs when $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}t\right)$ has its maximum value.

$$\therefore\ t=0 \text{ and } t=8$$
criteria: Gives partial justification or answer, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: When giving the reason $v=0$, care must be taken.
meta.format_note: Added the line integrating velocity to displacement to support the source's statement.

parts.latex:
A bag contains five red marbles and four blue marbles.

Three marbles are drawn in succession.

At each draw, if the marble is red it is replaced, and if it is blue it is not replaced.

Find the probability of drawing: one red marble.

solutions.latex:
Tree diagram (1st, 2nd, 3rd draw). After a red draw the marble is replaced, so the probabilities stay $\dfrac59$ red and $\dfrac49$ blue. After a blue draw there are 8 marbles ($\dfrac58$ red, $\dfrac38$ blue). After two blue draws there are 7 marbles ($\dfrac57$ red, $\dfrac27$ blue).

Exactly one red marble can occur in three ways:
$$\begin{aligned} P(RBB)&=\dfrac59\times\dfrac49\times\dfrac38=\dfrac{5}{54} \\ P(BRB)&=\dfrac49\times\dfrac58\times\dfrac38=\dfrac{5}{48} \\ P(BBR)&=\dfrac49\times\dfrac38\times\dfrac57=\dfrac{5}{42} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{1 red})=\dfrac{5}{54}+\dfrac{5}{48}+\dfrac{5}{42}=\dfrac{955}{3024}$$

meta.format_note: Tree diagram described in words in the source; the guideline's tree is not drawn here but the probabilities are all stated in the working.

parts.latex: Prove that $\dfrac{\tan\theta+1}{\sec\theta}-\dfrac{\operatorname{cosec}\theta}{\cot\theta+\tan\theta}=\sin\theta$.

solutions.latex:
Express everything in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, using $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$, $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ and $\cot\theta=\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=\cos\theta\left(\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}+1\right)-\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\left(\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}+\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)} \\ &=\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\left(\frac{\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\right)} \\ &=\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta\left(\frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\right)} \\ &=\sin\theta+\cos\theta-\cos\theta \\ &=\sin\theta \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Changes into $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\tan x}\right)$ and hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\pi} 3\sec^2 x\cdot e^{\tan x}\,dx$. Leave your answer in the exact form.

solutions.latex:
By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\tan x}\right)=\sec^2 x\, e^{\tan x}$$
Hence $e^{\tan x}$ is a primitive of $\sec^2 x\, e^{\tan x}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\pi}3\sec^2 x\, e^{\tan x}\,dx&=3\left[e^{\tan x}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\pi} \\ &=3\left[e^{\tan\pi}-e^{\tan\frac{\pi}{3}}\right] \\ &=3\left[e^0-e^{\sqrt3}\right] \\ &=3\left(1-e^{\sqrt3}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct derivative or primitive, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: The integral runs from $\frac{\pi}{3}$ to $\pi$, which passes through $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ where $\tan x$ is undefined, so the integrand is discontinuous there; the source ignores this.

4822.stem: A particle starts from the origin and moves in a straight line with a velocity given by $v=\dfrac{3t}{5+t^2}$ metres per second, where $t$ is in seconds.

parts.latex: Find an expression for the acceleration. Simplify your answer.
Describe the motion of the particle initially. In your answer, make reference to the velocity and to the acceleration of the particle.

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3t & v&=5+t^2 \\ u'&=3 & v'&=2t \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{(5+t^2)(3)-(3t)(2t)}{(5+t^2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{15+3t^2-6t^2}{(5+t^2)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{15-3t^2}{(5+t^2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the quotient rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} v&=0 \\ a&=\dfrac{15}{25}=\dfrac35 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the particle is initially at rest, and its velocity will increase due to the positive acceleration of $0.6\text{ m/s}^2$.
criteria: Finds velocity and acceleration at $t=0$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The top of a tower $B$ is due north of Patricia ($P$) and its angle of elevation is $42^\circ$. From Queenie ($Q$) who is $80$ metres from Patricia, the tower is due west and its angle of elevation is $38^\circ$. Let the height of the tower be $h$ metres and let $C$ be the base of the tower on the ground. Calculate the height of the tower, correct to one decimal place.

\exfigure{1317_q14b_1}
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tower seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1317_q14b_s1}

The angles of depression/elevation give $\angle PBC=48^\circ$ and $\angle QBC=52^\circ$ in the vertical triangles (angle sum with the right angle at $C$).

In $\triangle PBC$: $PC=h\tan 48^\circ$.

In $\triangle QBC$: $QC=h\tan 52^\circ$.

P is due south of $C$ and Q is due east of $C$, so $\triangle PCQ$ is right-angled at $C$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} PC^2+QC^2&=PQ^2 \\ h^2\tan^2 48^\circ+h^2\tan^2 52^\circ&=80^2 \\ h^2&=\dfrac{80^2}{\tan^2 48^\circ+\tan^2 52^\circ} \\ h&=\sqrt{2228.636719} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{height of tower}\approx 47.2\text{ m}$$

4824.stem: The cost of riding a Harley-Davidson motor bike (in dollars per hour) depends on the speed ($v$) of the motor bike (in kilometres per hour) and is given by $C=3v^2+15v+20000$.

parts.latex: Show that the total cost for a trip of $90$ km is given by: $P=270v+1350+\dfrac{1800000}{v}$
Find the speed, in km/h, that will minimise the cost of this trip

solutions.latex:
The cost per hour is $C=3v^2+15v+20000$. A trip of $90$ km at speed $v$ takes $t=\dfrac{90}{v}$ hours.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\dfrac{90}{v}\times C \\ &=\dfrac{90}{v}\left(3v^2+15v+20000\right) \\ &=270v+1350+\dfrac{1800000}{v} \end{aligned}$$

For minimum cost, $\dfrac{dP}{dv}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dv}&=270-\dfrac{1800000}{v^2}=0 \\ v^2&=\dfrac{1800000}{270}=\dfrac{20000}{3} \end{aligned}$$
Since $v>0$:
$$v=\sqrt{\dfrac{20000}{3}}\approx 81.6\text{ km/h}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative:
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dv^2}=\dfrac{3600000}{v^3}$$
When $v=81.6$:
$$\dfrac{d^2P}{dv^2}=\dfrac{3600000}{81.6^3}\approx 6.6>0$$
so this is a minimum.

$$\therefore\ v\approx 81.6\text{ km/h minimises the cost}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $v$, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

In the diagram above, what is the area of the shaded region?

solutions.latex:
The region lies below the $x$-axis between $x=0$ and $x=2$, so the integral is negative.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 (x^2-4)\,dx &= \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} - 4x\right]_0^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{8}{3} - 8\right) - (0-0) \\ &= -\dfrac{16}{3} \end{aligned}$$
By symmetry the shaded area is twice this magnitude.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2 \times \dfrac{16}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{32}{3} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex: What is the limiting sum of the series $\dfrac{13}{6}, \dfrac{13}{36}, \dfrac{13}{216}, \ldots$?

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with first term and common ratio
$$a = \dfrac{13}{6}, \quad r = \dfrac{1}{6}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{6} \div \dfrac{5}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{5} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex: Which expression is equal to $\displaystyle\int \dfrac{4}{1-\sin^2 4x}\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
Using $1-\sin^2 4x = \cos^2 4x$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int \dfrac{4}{1-\sin^2 4x}\,dx &= \int \dfrac{4}{\cos^2 4x}\,dx \\ &= \int 4\sec^2(4x)\,dx \\ &= 4 \times \dfrac{1}{4}\tan 4x + C \\ &= \tan 4x + C \end{aligned}$$
This matches option C.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $\dfrac{e^{2-x}}{x^2}$?

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2-x} & v&=x^2\\ u'&=-e^{2-x} & v'&=2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2} \\ &= \dfrac{-x^2e^{2-x} - 2xe^{2-x}}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{-xe^{2-x}(x+2)}{x^4} \\ &= \dfrac{-e^{2-x}(x+2)}{x^3} \end{aligned}$$
This equals $\dfrac{-2e^{2-x} - xe^{2-x}}{x^3}$, option B.

parts.latex:
A function is defined by the rule

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } x < 1 \\ x + 2 & \text{for } x \ge 1 \end{cases}$$

Which statement is incorrect?

solutions.latex:
For $x \ge 1$, $f(x) = x+2 \ge 3$, and $f(x) = 1$ for $x < 1$.

So the range is $\{1\} \cup [3, \infty)$, not $f(x) \ge 1$.

parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - 9}}$?

solutions.latex:
The square root is in the denominator, so we need $x^2 - 9 > 0$.

Hence $x < -3$ or $x > 3$, which is $(-\infty, -3) \cup (3, \infty)$, option A.

parts.latex: Using the trapezoidal rule with 4 subintervals, which expression gives the best approximation of the area under the curve $y = xe^{2x}$ between $x = 1$ and $x = 2$?

$$h = \dfrac{2-1}{4} = 0.25$$
\extable{Ts7167_1}

Using the trapezoidal rule:
$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{0.25}{2}\left(e^2 + 2(1.25e^{2.5}) + 2(1.5e^3) + 2(1.75e^{3.5}) + 2e^4\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{8}\left(e^2 + 2.5e^{2.5} + 3e^3 + 3.5e^{3.5} + 2e^4\right) \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: What is the nature and coordinates of the stationary point of the curve $y = \dfrac{\ln x}{x^3}$?

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\ln x & v&=x^3\\ u'&=\dfrac{1}{x} & v'&=3x^2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2 - 3x^2\ln x}{x^6} \\ &= \dfrac{1 - 3\ln x}{x^4} \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur when $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 - 3\ln x &= 0 \\ \ln x &= \dfrac{1}{3} \\ x &= e^{\frac{1}{3}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{\ln e^{\frac{1}{3}}}{\left(e^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3e} \end{aligned}$$
The stationary point is a maximum turning point at $\left(e^{\frac{1}{3}}, \dfrac{1}{3e}\right)$, option D.

meta.format_note: Source did not test the nature; the keyed option is stated without a test (sign of $y'$ changes from positive to negative since numerator $1-3\ln x$ decreases).

parts.latex: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = x^3 - x + 4$ at $x = 1$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate to find the gradient:
$$y' = 3x^2 - 1$$
At $x = 1$, the gradient is $y' = 2$.

When $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 1 - 1 + 4 \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
So the point is $(1, 4)$.
$$\begin{aligned} y - 4 &= 2(x - 1) \\ y &= 2x + 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y = 2x + 2$$
criteria: Finds the gradient or the point of tangency, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Differentiate $y = \sqrt{x}$.

$$\begin{aligned} y &= x^{\frac{1}{2}} \\ y' &= \dfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \end{aligned}$$

Total sales are $\$25\,000$, and Saturday plus Sunday is $\$14\,000$.

So the week days total
$$\begin{aligned} 25\,000 - 14\,000 &= 11\,000 \end{aligned}$$

Reading the Pareto chart at Sunday gives about $56\%$ for the weekend, so $44\%$ for the week days. The chart reading is not very accurate.

A sale early in the week to encourage customers.

Close on a Monday.

Longer trading hours on weekends.

parts.latex: If $\cos\theta = -\dfrac{3}{7}$ and $\tan\theta$ is positive, find the value of $\sin\theta$. Leave your answer in simplified form.

solutions.latex:
In a right triangle with hypotenuse 7 and adjacent side 3, let the opposite side be $x$. By Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 + 3^2 &= 7^2 \\ x^2 &= 40 \\ x &= \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10} \end{aligned}$$
So the acute reference angle $\alpha$ has $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}$.

Since $\cos\theta < 0$ and $\tan\theta > 0$, $\theta$ is in Quadrant 3, where sine is negative.
$$\therefore\ \sin\theta = -\dfrac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}$$
criteria: Finds the magnitude of $\sin\theta$ or the correct quadrant, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: How many terms are there in the series $11 + 13 + 15 + \cdots$ if the sum is 375?

solutions.latex:
This is an arithmetic series with $a = 11$ and $d = 2$.

Using the sum formula $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left(2a + (n-1)d\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 375 &= \dfrac{n}{2}\left(22 + (n-1)2\right) \\ 750 &= n(20 + 2n) \\ 2n^2 + 20n - 750 &= 0 \\ n^2 + 10n - 375 &= 0 \\ (n - 15)(n + 25) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $n = 15$ or $n = -25$.

Since $n > 0$, $n = 15$.
$$\therefore\ \text{There are 15 terms.}$$
criteria: Forms the quadratic equation in $n$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: triangle ABC: C 12 km due north of A, B at 050 degrees T and 9 km from A

parts.latex: Find the distance $BC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
What is the true bearing of $C$ from $B$? Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.

solutions.latex:
Using the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$, with $\angle BAC = 50^\circ$, $AC = 12$ and $AB = 9$:
$$\begin{aligned} BC^2 &= 12^2 + 9^2 - 2 \times 12 \times 9\cos 50^\circ \\ &= 86.157\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ BC \approx 9.28 \text{ km}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none). Diagram of the question's figure is given; no solution diagram added.

solutions.latex:
Let $\angle ACB = \theta$. Using the sine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{9}{\sin\theta} &= \dfrac{BC}{\sin 50^\circ} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{9\sin 50^\circ}{BC} \\ &= 0.7428\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\theta \approx 48^\circ$$
Ambiguous case check: the other angle is $180^\circ - 48^\circ = 132^\circ$, and $132^\circ + 50^\circ > 180^\circ$, so $\theta$ is acute.

Since $C$ is north-west of $B$, the bearing of $C$ from $B$ is
$$360^\circ - 48^\circ = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
Alternatively, let $\angle ABC = \alpha$:
$$\sin\alpha = \dfrac{12\sin 50^\circ}{BC} = 0.9903\ldots$$
so $\alpha = 82^\circ$, and the bearing is
$$82^\circ + 50^\circ + 180^\circ = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{bearing} = 312^\circ \text{ T}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle ACB$ or $\angle ABC$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

$$\begin{aligned} 4 &= 5\log_a x - 3\log_a x \\ &= 2\log_a x \end{aligned}$$
So $\log_a x = 2$.

parts.latex: Find the stationary points of the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$. Determine their nature.
Show that there is an inflection point at $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{32}{27}\right)$ on the curve.
For what interval is the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$ increasing?
Hence, sketch the graph of the curve $y = 4x^2 - 2x^3$. Clearly label the stationary points, the point of inflection and any intercepts with the axes.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate:
$$\begin{aligned} y' &= 8x - 6x^2 = 2x(4 - 3x) \\ y'' &= 8 - 12x \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $y' = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = \dfrac{4}{3}$.

The sign of $y''$ decides the nature.
$$\begin{aligned} x = 0:\ & y'' = 8 > 0 &&\text{concave up, so } (0,0) \text{ is a minimum turning point} \\ x = \dfrac{4}{3}:\ & y'' = 8 - 12 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = -8 < 0 &&\text{concave down, so a maximum turning point} \end{aligned}$$
When $x = \dfrac{4}{3}$:
$$y = 4\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^2 - 2\left(\dfrac{4}{3}\right)^3 = \dfrac{64}{27}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum at } (0,0),\ \text{maximum at } \left(\dfrac{4}{3}, \dfrac{64}{27}\right)$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points and tests one, or equivalent merit
Finds $y'$ and $x = 0$ or $x = \dfrac{4}{3}$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Inflection points occur where $y'' = 0$:
$$8 - 12x = 0$$
so $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Test the concavity either side of $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

\extable{Ts7188_1}

The concavity changes at $x = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so there is an inflection point there, with $y = \dfrac{32}{27}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{inflection point at } \left(\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{32}{27}\right)$$
criteria: Correct answer, showing the change in concavity

4849.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x = 12\ln(t + 2) - 2t + 5,$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds.

parts.latex: What is the initial position of the particle? Give your answer in exact form.
Find the expression for the velocity of the particle at time $t$.
Find the time when the particle is at rest.
What happens to the acceleration eventually?

solutions.latex:
At $t = 0$:
$$x = 12\ln 2 + 5$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is } (12\ln 2 + 5) \text{ metres to the right of } O$$
$$\begin{aligned} v &= \dfrac{dx}{dt} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{t + 2} - 2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
At rest, $v = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{t+2} - 2 &= 0 \\ \dfrac{12}{t+2} &= 2 \\ 12 &= 2t + 4 \\ 2t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 4 \text{ s}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Write $v = 12(t+2)^{-1} - 2$. Then
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{dv}{dt} \\ &= -12(t+2)^{-2} \\ &= -\dfrac{12}{(t+2)^2} \end{aligned}$$
As $t \to \infty$, $(t+2)^2 \to \infty$.
$$\therefore\ a \to 0$$

meta.marker_note: Also accept: as $t \to \infty$, $v \to$ constant, so zero acceleration.

parts.latex:
A curve $y = f(x)$ passes through $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{-\pi}{2}\right)$ and has the gradient function

$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 4\cos 2x + 1.$$

Find the equation of the curve.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the gradient function:
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \displaystyle\int (4\cos 2x + 1)\,dx \\ &= 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + x + C \\ &= 2\sin 2x + x + C \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}, -\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{\pi}{2} &= 2\sin\pi + \dfrac{\pi}{2} + C \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + C \end{aligned}$$
So $C = -\pi$.
$$\therefore\ y = 2\sin 2x + x - \pi$$
criteria: Correct integral with $C$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Solve the equation $2\sin 2x = 1$ for $0 \le x \le 2\pi$.

solutions.latex:
Let $u = 2x$. Since $0 \le x \le 2\pi$, we have $0 \le u \le 4\pi$.

Then $2\sin u = 1$, so $\sin u = \dfrac{1}{2}$, with related angle $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

Sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, over two revolutions:
$$u = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \dfrac{13\pi}{6}, \dfrac{17\pi}{6}$$
Since $x = \dfrac{u}{2}$:
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \dfrac{5\pi}{12}, \dfrac{13\pi}{12}, \dfrac{17\pi}{12}$$
criteria: Finds all four values of $u$, or equivalent merit
Finds $\sin u = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and a correct value of $u$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^5 \dfrac{x^2 + 3}{x}\,dx$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5 \dfrac{x^2 + 3}{x}\,dx &= \int_1^5 \left(x + \dfrac{3}{x}\right)dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} + 3\ln x\right]_1^5 \\ &= \dfrac{25}{2} + 3\ln 5 - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} + 3\ln 1\right) \\ &= 12 + 3\ln 5 \end{aligned}$$

4856.stem: Hugo has three years to save \$25\,000 for a holiday.

parts.latex: Hugo deposits a single lump sum into an account paying 8% p.a. interest compounded every 6 months. What lump sum is needed to ensure he can afford his holiday in three years time? Give your answer to the nearest dollar.

parts.note: Annuity look-up using a future value interest-factor table (2024 Advanced uses the GP formula only)

solutions.latex:
The interest rate per period is $R = 4\%$ per 6 months, and the number of periods is $n = 3 \times 2 = 6$.

Using the compound interest formula, $FV = PV(1+R)^n$:
$$PV \times (1.04)^6 = 25\,000$$
$$\begin{aligned} PV &= \dfrac{25\,000}{1.04^6} \\ &\approx \$19\,758 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct rate and number of periods, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The rate per quarter is $R = \dfrac{12\%}{4} = 3\%$, and the number of quarters is $n = 3 \times 4 = 12$.

The table value for $3\%$ and $12$ periods is $14.1920$.
$$\begin{aligned} FV &= 1800 \times 14.1920 \\ &= \$25\,546 \end{aligned}$$
Since $\$25\,546 > \$25\,000$, Hugo has enough money for his holiday.
criteria: Some appropriate working ($3\%$ per quarter, $12$ periods, table value), or equivalent merit

4857.stem: A closed cylindrical tank has a circular base of radius $r$ metres and a height of $h$ metres. It can hold $160\pi\ \text{m}^3$ of wheat. The material for the flat circular top and bottom costs \$10 per square metre and the material for the curved surface costs \$8 per square metre.

parts.latex: Show that the height of the tank is $h = \dfrac{160}{r^2}$.
Find the dimensions of the tank that minimise the cost of construction.

solutions.latex:
The volume of a cylinder is $V = \pi r^2 h$, and the tank holds $160\pi \text{ m}^3$.
$$160\pi = \pi r^2 h$$
$$\therefore\ h = \dfrac{160}{r^2}$$

solutions.latex:
The top and bottom are two circles of area $\pi r^2$, at \$10 per square metre.
$$\text{Cost} = 2 \times \pi r^2 \times 10 = 20\pi r^2$$
The curved surface has area $2\pi r h$, and $h = \dfrac{160}{r^2}$, at \$8 per square metre.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= 2\pi r \times \dfrac{160}{r^2} = \dfrac{320\pi}{r} \\ \text{Cost} &= \dfrac{320\pi}{r} \times 8 = \dfrac{2560\pi}{r} \end{aligned}$$
The total cost is
$$C = 20\pi r^2 + 2560\pi r^{-1}$$
Differentiating,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dC}{dr} &= 40\pi r - 2560\pi r^{-2} \\ C'' &= 40\pi + \dfrac{5120\pi}{r^3} \end{aligned}$$
For a stationary point, $\dfrac{dC}{dr} = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2560\pi}{r^2} &= 40\pi r \\ r^3 &= 64 \\ r &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
When $r = 4$,
$$C'' = 40\pi + \dfrac{5120\pi}{64} > 0$$
so this is a minimum.

The height is
$$h = \dfrac{160}{4^2} = 10 \text{ m}$$
$$\therefore\ r = 4 \text{ m and } h = 10 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct nature test and dimensions with minor error, or equivalent merit
Correct derivative of the cost function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Prove the identity $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta}$.

solutions.latex:
Rewrite in terms of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$, then use $\cos^2\theta = 1 - \sin^2\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= (\sec\theta + \tan\theta)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{\cos^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{1 - \sin^2\theta} \\ &= \dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)^2}{(1 - \sin\theta)(1 + \sin\theta)} \\ &= \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta} \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the left side as $\dfrac{(1+\sin\theta)^2}{\cos^2\theta}$, or equivalent merit

4859.stem:
Tom invented a dice game to play on his own. He throws a pair of six-sided dice repeatedly until the difference between the dice is 2 or 3.

If the difference is 2, Tom wins and the game ends.

If the difference is 3, Tom loses and the game ends.

If the difference is any other number, he continues to throw until the difference is a 2 or 3.

parts.latex: Show that the probability that Tom wins on his first throw of the dice is $\dfrac{2}{9}$.
Calculate the probability that the game continues to a second throw.
What is the probability that Tom wins in one of the first three throws? Leave your answer in unsimplified form.
Calculate the probability that Tom wins the game.

solutions.latex:
The difference is $2$ for the pairs $(1,3),(2,4),(3,5),(4,6)$ and their reverses, so $8$ of the $36$ equally likely outcomes.
$$P(\text{win on first throw}) = \dfrac{8}{36} = \dfrac{2}{9}$$
criteria: Some appropriate working, or equivalent merit

meta.source_flag: Guideline drawing not cropped: table of the difference between the two dice (die 1 across, die 2 up), showing the difference is 2 in 8 of 36 outcomes.
meta.format_note: Pairs listed to give the count of 8 in words.

solutions.latex:
The difference is $3$ for the pairs $(1,4),(2,5),(3,6)$ and their reverses, which is $6$ outcomes.
$$P(\text{difference } 2 \text{ or } 3) = \dfrac{8 + 6}{36} = \dfrac{14}{36}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{continue}) &= 1 - \dfrac{14}{36} \\ &= \dfrac{11}{18} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Tom wins on throw $1$, or continues once and wins on throw $2$, or continues twice and wins on throw $3$.
$$P = \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{2}{9} + \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{11}{18} \times \dfrac{2}{9}$$
This simplifies to $\dfrac{643}{1458}$.
criteria: Writes one or two correct terms, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The probabilities of winning on throw $1, 2, 3, \dots$ form a geometric series with first term $a = \dfrac{2}{9}$ and common ratio $r = \dfrac{11}{18}$.

Since $|r| < 1$, the sum to infinity exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S_\infty &= \dfrac{a}{1 - r} \\ &= \dfrac{\frac{2}{9}}{1 - \frac{11}{18}} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{9} \times \dfrac{18}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{7} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the geometric series, or equivalent merit

4860.stem:
On the 1st January 2021, Amanda invested \$7000 into a bank account that paid interest at a rate of 6% p.a. compounded annually. Amanda decided to add \$700 to her account on the 1st January each year, beginning in 2022.

Let $A_n$ be the amount in the account on the 1st January after $n$ years, after interest and her deposit has been paid.

parts.latex: Show that $A_2 = A_1 \times 1.06 + 700$.
Hence, determine how much was in her account on 1st January 2031, after interest and her deposit has been paid. Give your answer to the nearest dollar.

Amanda's friend, Bard, invested \$7000 into an account in a different bank on the 1st January 2021 and made no further payments. On 1st January 2031, Bard's balance was \$23\,417.

Calculate the annual rate of compound interest paid on Bard's account. Give your answer to 4 significant figures.

solutions.latex:
$A_1$ is the opening amount after one year's interest and the deposit.
$$A_1 = 7000 \times 1.06 + 700$$
In the second year the balance earns $6\%$ interest and then $\$700$ is added.
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= A_1 + 0.06A_1 + 700 \\ &= A_1 \times 1.06 + 700 \end{aligned}$$
Expanding,
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= (7000 \times 1.06 + 700) \times 1.06 + 700 \\ &= 7000 \times 1.06^2 + 700 \times 1.06 + 700 \end{aligned}$$

Continuing the pattern,
$$A_3 = 7000 \times 1.06^3 + 700 \times 1.06^2 + 700 \times 1.06 + 700$$
$$A_n = 7000 \times 1.06^n + 700 \times 1.06^{n-1} + \cdots + 700 \times 1.06 + 700$$
The terms after the first form a geometric series with $a = 700$, $r = 1.06$ and $n$ terms.
$$A_n = 7000 \times 1.06^n + \dfrac{700(1.06^n - 1)}{0.06}$$
1st January 2031 is $10$ years after 2021, so $n = 10$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{10} &= 7000 \times 1.06^{10} + \dfrac{700(1.06^{10} - 1)}{0.06} \\ &\approx \$21\,762 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies the pattern and the geometric series, or equivalent merit
Writes $A_3$ or the general pattern, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Bard's balance after $10$ years at $R\%$ p.a. compounded annually is given by
$$7000\left(1 + \dfrac{R}{100}\right)^{10} = 23\,417$$
Taking the tenth root,
$$\begin{aligned} 1 + \dfrac{R}{100} &= \sqrt[10]{\dfrac{23\,417}{7000}} \\ \dfrac{R}{100} &= \sqrt[10]{\dfrac{23\,417}{7000}} - 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ R \approx 12.83\%$$

parts.latex: Find the area bounded by the curves $y = \sqrt{4x + 8}$ and $5y - 2x = 12$.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1318_q33_s1}

The line is $y = \dfrac{2x + 12}{5}$. At the intersections,
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{4x+8} &= \dfrac{2x + 12}{5} \\ 10\sqrt{x+2} &= 2x + 12 \\ 100(x+2) &= (2x+12)^2 \\ 4x^2 - 52x - 56 &= 0 \\ x^2 - 13x - 14 &= 0 \\ (x+1)(x-14) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = -1 \text{ or } x = 14$$
The curve $y = \sqrt{4x+8}$ is above the line $y = \dfrac{2}{5}x + \dfrac{12}{5}$ between the intersection points.
$$A = \int_{-1}^{14}\left(\sqrt{4x+8} - \left(\dfrac{2}{5}x + \dfrac{12}{5}\right)\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \left[\dfrac{(4x+8)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6} - \dfrac{x^2}{5} - \dfrac{12x}{5}\right]_{-1}^{14} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{256}{3} - \dfrac{196}{5} - \dfrac{168}{5}\right) - \left(\dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{12}{5}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{252}{3} - \dfrac{375}{5} \\ &= 84 - 75 \\ &= 9 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Estragon has scored $90\%, 78\%, 81\%,$ and $83\%$ on his first four class tests. After the fifth class test, his mean mark is increased by $1\%$.

What was Estragon's mark in his fifth class test ?
parts.note: Mean of a raw data set (summary statistics) has no 2024 Advanced dot point; Y11 Data only names mode and median.

solutions.latex:
The mean of the first four tests is
$$\dfrac{90+78+81+83}{4} = \dfrac{332}{4} = 83\%$$
The new mean is $84\%$. Let $x$ be the fifth mark.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x+332}{5} &= 84 \\ x &= 5\times 84 - 332 \\ &= 88\% \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: Which of the following is equal to $\dfrac{\log_4 16}{\log_4 2}$ ?

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\log_4 16}{\log_4 2} &= \dfrac{\log_4 2^4}{\log_4 2} \\ &= \dfrac{4\log_4 2}{\log_4 2} \\ &= 4 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex:
The function $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ is translated 3 units up and 2 units right to produce $y = g(x)$.

Which of the following is the equation of the translated function $g(x)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Translating 2 units right replaces $x$ with $x-2$, and 3 units up adds $3$.
$$g(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-2} + 3$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: Given that $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{2}$ for $0 < \theta < \pi$, what is the exact value of $\sin\theta$ ?

solutions.latex:
Since $\tan\theta = \dfrac{3}{2}$, draw a right-angled triangle with opposite side $3$ and adjacent side $2$. By Pythagoras' theorem, the hypotenuse is
$$\sqrt{3^2+2^2} = \sqrt{13}$$
$\tan\theta$ is positive, so $\theta$ is in quadrant 1 or 3. Since $0<\theta<\pi$, it is in quadrant 1, where $\sin\theta$ is positive.
$$\sin\theta = \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}$$
This is option B.

4883.stem:
Atticus owns a biased six-sided die which has the following discrete probability distribution

\extable{1319_q22_t1}

parts.latex: Find $P(3 < X \le 6)$
Show that the expected value $E(X) = 2.85$

At a school fund raiser, Atticus uses his biased die to run a game, where students pay \$3.50 per game to roll the biased die and in turn win \$1 multiplied by the number that they have rolled

How much profit or loss would Atticus expect to make for 200 games?

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} P(3<X\le 6) &= 0.1+0.1+0.1 \\ &= 0.3 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= 1\times 0.25 + 2\times 0.25 + 3\times 0.2 + 4\times 0.1 + 5\times 0.1 + 6\times 0.1 \\ &= 2.85 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Each game wins $\$X$, so the expected payout is $E(X)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Expected profit per game} &= \$3.50 - \$2.85 \\ &= \$0.65 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Expected profit for 200 games} &= 200\times\$0.65 \\ &= \$130 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Atticus expects a profit of } \$130$$
criteria: Finds the expected profit per game, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

4884.stem: The 2021 Semester one report marks for a Year 12 Advanced Mathematics cohort at a particular selective boys high school is normally distributed with a mean of 76 and a standard deviation of 11

parts.latex: What is the probability that a randomly selected student from the cohort will have a mark between 54 and 98 ?
A student is selected randomly from the cohort. What is the probability that his mark is less than or equal to 65?

solutions.latex:
$54=\mu-2\sigma$ and $98=\mu+2\sigma$, so by the empirical rule the probability is the proportion within 2 standard deviations of the mean.
$$\therefore\ P(54\le X\le 98) = 95\%$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$65=\mu-\sigma$. By the empirical rule, $34\%$ of scores lie between $\mu-\sigma$ and $\mu$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(X\le 65) &= 50\% - 34\% \\ &= 16\% \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Prove that $(\sin x + \cos x)(\sec x - \operatorname{cosec} x) = \tan x - \cot x$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= (\sin x+\cos x)(\sec x - \operatorname{cosec} x) \\ &= \sin x\sec x + \cos x\sec x - \sin x\operatorname{cosec} x - \cos x\operatorname{cosec} x \\ &= \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} + \dfrac{\cos x}{\cos x} - \dfrac{\sin x}{\sin x} - \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x} \\ &= \tan x + 1 - 1 - \cot x \\ &= \tan x - \cot x \\ &= \text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Expands and writes in terms of $\sin x$ and $\cos x$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\int x(x^2 + 5)^9\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the integrand in the form $\displaystyle\int f'(x)[f(x)]^n\,dx$ with $f(x)=x^2+5$, $f'(x)=2x$, $n=9$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int x(x^2+5)^9\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int 2x(x^2+5)^9\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{n+1}[f(x)]^{n+1} + C \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{1}{10}(x^2+5)^{10} + C \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \int x(x^2+5)^9\,dx = \dfrac{(x^2+5)^{10}}{20} + C$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

parts.latex:
Five values of a function $f(x)$ are shown in in the table below.

\extable{1319_q26_t1}

Use the trapezoidal rule with the five values given in the table to estimate

$$\int_{20}^{40} f(x)\,dx$$

solutions.latex:
There are $5$ function values, so $n=4$ subintervals (not the number of values), with width $h=\dfrac{40-20}{4}=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{20}^{40}f(x)\,dx &\approx \dfrac{1}{2}\times 5\times\{10+20+2\times(12+25+28)\} \\ &= 400 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes correctly into the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
Finds the strip width $5$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Table values taken from source working.

parts.latex: Differentiate $y = xe^{2x}$
Hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_0^2 e^{2x}(3 + 6x)\,dx$

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=e^{2x}\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2e^{2x}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= e^{2x} + 2xe^{2x} \\ &= (1+2x)e^{2x} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From part (a), $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(xe^{2x}\right)=(1+2x)e^{2x}$, so $xe^{2x}$ is an antiderivative of $e^{2x}(1+2x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 e^{2x}(3+6x)\,dx &= 3\int_0^2 e^{2x}(1+2x)\,dx \\ &= 3\left[xe^{2x}\right]_0^2 \\ &= 3\times(2e^{4} - 0) \\ &= 6e^4 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

4889.stem:
The following table shows the number of absences from class versus the common test mark in a mathematics class of 11 students (student Joseph K missed the test and so does not appear in the table)

\extable{1319_q28_t1}

parts.latex: Find the equation of the least-squares line of best fit in terms of number of absences ($n$) and the mark ($m$) (correct to 3 decimal places)
parts.note: Least-squares regression (bivariate data) is not in 2024 Advanced; it is Standard content.

parts.latex:
Student Josef K who missed the test, was absent from 13 maths lessons in total. His teacher estimated his mark using the equation of the line of best fit.

What was Josef's estimated mark? (correct to the nearest whole number)
parts.note: Prediction from a least-squares regression line is not in 2024 Advanced; it is Standard content.

solutions.latex:
Using the calculator's least-squares regression, $y=A+Bx$ with $A=90.920$ and $B=-3.455$.
$$\therefore\ m = -3.455n + 90.920$$
where $n$ is the number of absences and $m$ is the mark.
criteria: Finds one of the coefficients correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} m &= -3.455\times 13 + 90.920 \\ &\approx 46 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{estimated mark} = 46$$

4890.stem:
The temperature of a freshly served bowl of phở bò from Tan Viet Noodle House is given by the following equation:

$$T = 22 + 60e^{-0.1t}$$

Where $T$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius

And $t$ is the time in minutes.

parts.latex: To the nearest degree, what is the temperature of the phở after 1 minute ?
How long will it take for the temperature of the phở to drop to $62^\circ$

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 22 + 60e^{-0.1\times 1} \\ &= 76.2\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ T \approx 76^\circ \text{C}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Put $T=62$.
$$\begin{aligned} 62 &= 22 + 60e^{-0.1t} \\ 60e^{-0.1t} &= 40 \\ e^{-0.1t} &= \dfrac{2}{3} \\ -0.1t &= \ln\dfrac{2}{3} \\ t &\approx 4.05 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 4.05 \text{ minutes (4 minutes 3 seconds)}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

Use the following standard Z-table for this question.

parts.latex: What is $P(X \le 1.8)$ ?
What is $P(-1.2 \le X \le 0.3)$ ?

The birthweight of babies is known to be normally distributed. According to data which covers Australian pregnancies between 1998 and 2007, the mean ($\mu$) birthweight for boys was 3632 grams with a standard deviation ($\sigma$) of 430 grams.

What is the probability that a randomly selected newborn boy will weigh less than 3890 grams ?

solutions.latex:
From the Z-table,
$$P(X\le 1.8) = 0.9641$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. The Z-table figure is in the question.
Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Convert to a $z$-score using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.
$$z = \dfrac{3890-3632}{430} = 0.6$$
From the Z-table,
$$P(X\le 3890) = P(Z\le 0.6) = 0.7257$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: Sketch of f(x) with stationary points and point of inflexion

parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ has 2 stationary points at $P\,(1,-5)$ and $Q(-3,27)$ and determine their nature
Find any points of inflexion

Sketch the graph marking and labelling any stationary points or points of inflexion.

Do NOT determine the $x$ intercepts of the curve

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 3x^2+6x-9 \\ &= 3(x+3)(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
So $f'(x)=0$ gives $x=-3$ or $x=1$.
$$f(-3) = (-3)^3 + 3(-3)^2 - 9(-3) = 27$$
$$f(1) = 1+3-9 = -5$$
Hence the stationary points are $(-3,27)$ and $(1,-5)$, as required.

Nature (sign of $f'(x)$ either side):

\extable{Ts7262_1}

$\therefore\ (-3,27)$ is a local maximum and $(1,-5)$ is a local minimum.
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds $f'(x)$ and solves $f'(x)=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Kept \extable from source. Part (c) sketch is under sketch id 1319_q31_s2, not part of this solution.

solutions.latex:
Points of inflexion occur where $f''(x)=0$ with a change in concavity.
$$f''(x) = 6x+6 = 0 \text{ so } x=-1$$
$$y = (-1)^3+3(-1)^2-9(-1) = 11$$
Concavity changes at $x=-1$, since $f''(x)=6(x+1)$ changes sign there.

$$\therefore\ (-1,11) \text{ is a point of inflexion}$$

meta.format_note: Source justified by $f''(-1)=0$ and $f'(-1)\ne0$; replaced with the sign change of $f''$, which is the standard test. Rubric written by us.
