4893.stem:
A continuous random variable $X$ has a probability density function $f(x)$ given by

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} & \text{for } 1 \le x \le 2 \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function
Find $P(1.6 \le X \le 2)$
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^x f(t)\,dt$ for $1\le x\le 2$.

$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_1^x\left(\dfrac{t}{2}+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{4}+\dfrac{t}{4}\right]_1^x \\ &= \dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{x}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} \end{aligned}$$

For $x<1$, $F(x)=0$, and for $x>2$, $F(x)=1$.

$$\therefore\ F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x<1 \\[6pt] \dfrac{x^2+x-2}{4} & 1\le x\le 2 \\[6pt] 1 & x>2 \end{cases}$$
criteria: Integrates $f(x)$ from $1$ to $x$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave $F(x)=0$ otherwise; we wrote the cases $0$ for $x<1$ and $1$ for $x>2$ (standard CDF), which is the meaning of 'otherwise'. Used dummy variable $t$ in the integral (source reused $x$). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using $P(a\le X\le b)=F(b)-F(a)$:

$$\begin{aligned} P(1.6\le X\le 2) &= F(2)-F(1.6) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{2^2}{4}+\dfrac{2}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-\left(\dfrac{1.6^2}{4}+\dfrac{1.6}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ &= 0.46 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P(1.6\le X\le 2)=0.46 \left(=\dfrac{23}{50}\right)$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

4894.stem:
The graph of $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 4$ is shown below

parts.latex: On the diagram above, make an accurate sketch of $g(x) = -x^2 + x + 2$ marking the vertex and all intercepts

Hence, using the graphical method, find the number of solutions to the following equation

$$x^3 - 3x^2 + 4 = -x^2 + x + 2$$

solutions.latex:
Factorise $g(x)$ to find the intercepts.

$$\begin{aligned} g(x) &= -x^2+x+2 \\ &= -(x^2-x-2) \\ &= -(x-2)(x+1) \end{aligned}$$

The $x$-intercepts are $x=2$ and $x=-1$, and the $y$-intercept is $2$.

The vertex is at $x=\dfrac{-1+2}{2}=0.5$, and $y=-(0.5-2)(0.5+1)=2.25$, so the vertex is $(0.5,\,2.25)$.

\exfigure{1319_q33_s1}
criteria: Finds the vertex or the intercepts, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The solutions of $x^3-3x^2+4=-x^2+x+2$ are the $x$ values where the graphs of $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ intersect.

The graphs intersect at $3$ points.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are } 3 \text{ solutions}$$

parts.latex: Show that $h = 808$ metres to the nearest metre
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (mountain seen from two points on a road): now Year 11 Extension 1.

parts.latex: Find $OB$ to the nearest metre
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (mountain seen from two points on a road): now Year 11 Extension 1.

parts.latex: Hence, find the bearing of $O$ from $B$ (nearest degree)
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (mountain seen from two points on a road): now Year 11 Extension 1.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle $OAM$ (right angle at $O$), $\tan 22^\circ=\dfrac{OM}{OA}$.

$$\begin{aligned} h &= 2000\tan 22^\circ \\ &= 808.05\ldots \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ h = 808 \text{ m to the nearest metre}$$

meta.format_note: Source wrote $808.5$ before rounding to $808$; actual value of $2000\tan22^\circ$ is $808.05$, so I corrected the intermediate figure (final answer unchanged). Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle $OBM$ (right angle at $O$), $\tan 20^\circ=\dfrac{OM}{OB}$.

$$\begin{aligned} OB &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 20^\circ} \\ &= 2220.105\ldots \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ OB = 2220 \text{ m to the nearest metre}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1319_q34_s1}

In triangle $OAB$, $OB=2220$, $AB=1000$ and $OA=2000$. Using the cosine rule to find $\angle ABO$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos \angle ABO &= \dfrac{2220^2+1000^2-2000^2}{2\times 1000\times 2220} \\ &= 0.4343\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$$\angle ABO=\cos^{-1}(0.483\ldots)=64.257\ldots^\circ \approx 64^\circ$$

$A$ is due south of $B$, so the bearing of $O$ from $B$ is $180^\circ+\angle ABO$ (the mountain is to the left of the road, that is, west when travelling north).

$$\therefore\ \text{bearing} = 180^\circ+64^\circ = 244^\circ\text{T}$$
criteria: Uses the cosine rule in triangle $OAB$, or equivalent merit

4896.stem:
A tank initially holds 8100 litres of Water. The water drains from the bottom of the tank. A mathematical model predicts that the volume, $V$ litres, of water that will remain in the tank after $t$ minutes is given by

$$V = 8100\left(1 - \dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2$$

parts.latex: How long does the tank take to drain fully?
What volume does the model predict will remain after 20 minutes ?
At what rate does the model predict that the water will be draining from the tank after 30 minutes ?
At what time does the model predict that the water will drain from the tank at its fastest rate ?

solutions.latex:
The tank is fully drained when $V=0$.

$$8100\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^2=0$$

So $1-\dfrac{t}{90}=0$.

$$\therefore\ t=90 \text{ minutes}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} V &= 8100\left(1-\dfrac{20}{90}\right)^2 \\ &= 8100\times\left(\dfrac{7}{9}\right)^2 \\ &= 4900 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change of volume is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$. Differentiating using the chain rule:

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 8100\times 2\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{90}\right) \\ &= -180\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right) \\ &= 2t-180 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

At $t=30$:

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2\times 30-180=-120 \text{ L/min}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the water drains at } 120 \text{ L/min}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The rate is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2t-180$, so $\dfrac{d^2V}{dt^2}=2$.

Since $\dfrac{d^2V}{dt^2}\ne 0$, $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ has no stationary points and no points of inflexion. The greatest draining rate must therefore be at an endpoint of $0\le t\le 90$.

$$\begin{aligned} t=0 &: \dfrac{dV}{dt}=-180 \text{ L/min} \\ t=90 &: \dfrac{dV}{dt}=0 \text{ L/min} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the fastest draining rate is at } t=0$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

figures.cap: graphs of f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=(x-1)^2 with shaded region; top of y-axis label cropped

solutions.latex:
The shaded area is the area under $f(x)$ from $x=-1$ to $x=0$, plus the area under $g(x)$ from $x=0$ to $x=1$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^0 (x+1)\,dx+\int_0^1 (x-1)^2\,dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}+x\right]_{-1}^0+\left[\dfrac{(x-1)^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= 0-\left(\dfrac{(-1)^2}{2}-1\right)+\left(0-\dfrac{(-1)^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{5}{6} \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the correct integrals, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

Labels are in maths italic, including the x axis label, which is upright in the crop (rule 19). The axes have filled arrows at both ends. One difference: the left tail of f past A follows the true line, which is less steep than the crop's tail. Rules used: 1, 4, 5, 6, 9, 11, 12, 16, 19, 27.

4898.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line. Its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$v = 2 - \dfrac{4}{t+1}$$

parts.latex: Show that the particle is at rest when $t = 1$
The particle's initial displacement is 1 m. Find its displacement when at rest (3 decimal points)
Find the expression for the accelaration of the particle at time $t$
Explain why the displacement of the particle is always positive

solutions.latex:
At $t=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2-\dfrac{4}{1+1} \\ &= 2-2 \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest when } t=1$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(2-\dfrac{4}{t+1}\right)dt \\ &= 2t-4\ln(t+1)+C \end{aligned}$$

When $t=0$, $x=1$:

$$0-4\ln 1+C=1$$

So $C=1$ and $x=2t-4\ln(t+1)+1$.

At rest, $t=1$:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(1)-4\ln 2+1 \\ &= 3-4\ln 2 \\ &\approx 0.227 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{displacement} \approx 0.227 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the displacement function including the constant, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source used $d$ for displacement; written $x$ here. Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{dv}{dt} \\ &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(2-4(t+1)^{-1}\right) \\ &= 4(t+1)^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{4}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest only when $t=1$, so the displacement has only one stationary point, at $t=1$.

The acceleration there is $\dfrac{4}{(1+1)^2}=1>0$, so the displacement has a local minimum at $t=1$ (concave up).

The displacement at this minimum is $0.227>0$.

$$\therefore\ \text{displacement is always} \ge 0.227, \text{ so always positive}$$

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt} = 20000t - 12000$
Hence or otherwise find the minimum distance ($r$) between the cars (justify your answer with relevant mathematical arguments)

solutions.latex:
After $t$ hours, $RA=80t$ and $RB=100-60t$.

The roads meet at a right angle, so by Pythagoras' theorem in triangle $ARB$:

$$\begin{aligned} r^2 &= RB^2+RA^2 \\ &= (100-60t)^2+(80t)^2 \\ &= 10000-12000t+3600t^2+6400t^2 \\ &= 10000t^2-12000t+10000 \\ &= 2000(5t^2-6t+5) \end{aligned}$$

as required.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt} &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left[2000(5t^2-6t+5)\right] \\ &= 2000(10t-6) \\ &= 20000t-12000 \end{aligned}$$

as required.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
$r$ is a minimum when $r^2$ is a minimum.

Stationary point: $\dfrac{d(r^2)}{dt}=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 20000t-12000 &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{6}{10}=0.6 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

Nature: $\dfrac{d^2(r^2)}{dt^2}=20000>0$ for all $t$, so $r^2$ is concave up and the stationary point is a minimum.

$$\begin{aligned} r &= \sqrt{2000(5\times 0.6^2-6\times 0.6+5)} \\ &= \sqrt{6400} \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the minimum distance is } 80 \text{ km}$$

meta.format_note: Second derivative written as $20000$ (source wrote $2000(10)$, same value). Rubric written by us.

4900.stem:
Between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18, 2021, the height of the tide in Sydney harbour was given by

$$h(t) = 1 + 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) \text{ for } 0 \le t < 12$$

Where $h$ is the height of the tide in metres, and $t$ is in hours with $t = 0$ at 8 am

parts.latex: What is the period of $h(t)$
What was the height $h(t)$ at low tide, and at what time did this low tide occur
A cruise ship is only able to enter the harbour if the tide is at least 1.2 m. Find all the times between 8 am and 8 pm on July 18 2021 that the cruise ship was able to enter the harbour

solutions.latex:
For $h(t)=1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ with $b=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 2\pi\div\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 2\pi\times\dfrac{6}{\pi} \\ &= 12 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The minimum value of $\sin$ is $-1$, so the minimum height is $1-0.4=0.6$ m.

The sine curve reaches its minimum at $\dfrac{3}{4}$ of the period:

$$\dfrac{3}{4}\times 12=9 \text{ hours}$$

So the time is $8 \text{ am}+9 \text{ hours}=5$ pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{low tide is } 0.6 \text{ m at } 5 \text{ pm}$$
criteria: Finds the minimum height or the time of low tide, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
The ship can enter when $h\ge 1.2$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1+0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 1.2 \\ 0.4\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge 0.2 &&(\text{subtract } 1) \\ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) &\ge \dfrac{1}{2} &&(\text{divide by } 0.4) \end{aligned}$$

For $0\le t<12$, $0\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t<2\pi$, and $\sin\theta\ge\dfrac{1}{2}$ when $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\theta\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}\le\dfrac{\pi}{6}t &\le\dfrac{5\pi}{6} \\ 1\le t &\le 5 \end{aligned}$$

The times are $8+1=9$ am and $8+5=13$, that is, 1 pm.

$$\therefore\ \text{the ship can enter between 9 am and 1 pm}$$
